name: Hydroquinone-tretinoin-steroid triple cream (Kligman formula)

lead: The triple cream combines a skin-lightening agent (hydroquinone), a retinoid (tretinoin) and a topical steroid in one cream. It was devised in the 1970s by dermatologist Albert Kligman and is the standard topical for melasma, a chronic brown or grey facial pigmentation.

The branded fluocinolone version, Tri-Luma, has been tested in multicentre trials, and review articles describe it as more effective than hydroquinone alone. It is used to treat pigment disorders rather than to lighten normal skin.

paras: Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin. Tretinoin speeds skin turnover and aids penetration, and the steroid reduces irritation and inflammation from the other two. Together they are described as complementary.

Reported effects include local irritation, and long-term steroid and hydroquinone use are the concerns reviewers raise. The 12-month open-label study of the fluocinolone version reported a favourable safety profile. Hydroquinone regulation is tightening: in the US over-the-counter products were banned in 2020, and tretinoin should be avoided in pregnancy.

lead: The hydroquinone-tretinoin-steroid triple combination cream, often called the Kligman formula, is a topical prescription treatment for melasma and other hyperpigmentation. It combines the skin-lightening agent hydroquinone, the retinoid tretinoin and a corticosteroid.[1][2]

Hydroquinone use for hyperpigmentation was reported from 1936, and in 1975 dermatologist Albert Kligman tested a combination of 5 percent hydroquinone, 0.1 percent tretinoin and 0.1 percent dexamethasone for melasma.[3] A stable once-daily commercial formulation containing 4 percent hydroquinone, 0.05 percent tretinoin and 0.01 percent fluocinolone acetonide (Tri-Luma) was later tested in multicentre trials, which reviews describe as showing greater efficacy than its single components.[1][2]

General references report that the triple combination works better than dual therapy or hydroquinone alone, while also noting that melasma treatments often prove unsatisfying and that recurrence is common after sun exposure.[4]
infobox: Combination skin-lightening agent, retinoid and corticosteroid

paras: Melasma is a chronic, relapsing disorder of facial hyperpigmentation that is more common in women and in people with darker skin types. Hydroquinone is the best-known topical, with 2 percent available over the counter and 4 percent by prescription in some countries, and the triple combination is used as a first-line option.[4]

Expert commentary on melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation has also summarised management options, including combinations, sun protection and procedures.[5] The formulation has been tried in other conditions, including solar lentigines, post-sclerotherapy hyperpigmentation and, in a 2026 case report, a congenital epidermal nevus.[6][7]

A 12-month, multicentre, open-label study of the fluocinolone/hydroquinone/tretinoin cream enrolled 228 patients with facial melasma; 76 percent completed it, most patients had one or two treatment courses of about six months, and the authors reported a favourable safety profile.[1]

A comprehensive review of short- and long-term use described the cream as a stable, once-daily formulation of three established monotherapies for a condition that is hard to treat in darker complexions.[2] A cost-effectiveness analysis compared the fixed combination with hydroquinone alone applied twice daily in several countries using data from an 8-week trial.[8]

A 2025 randomised, single-centre, placebo-controlled trial compared a generic fluocinolone/hydroquinone/tretinoin cream with Tri-Luma in Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe melasma.[9] A 2022 randomised trial compared oral tranexamic acid plus the fluocinolone-based triple cream with the cream alone.[10]

Topical steroids and retinoids both have skin effects, and a registered study (completed 2006, n=70) examined the atrophogenic potential of the triple cream for melasma.[11] Tretinoin should be avoided in pregnancy.[4]

Hydroquinone has been the subject of safety concerns: encyclopedic sources report rat studies showing increased tumour rates, and the US FDA banned over-the-counter use in 2020, saying it could not rule out a carcinogenic potential.[3]

Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase and is a reducing agent and antioxidant.[3][4] Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover, and the corticosteroid component is intended to limit irritation from the others.[2][4]

Hydroquinone was obtained from quinic acid in 1820 and named in 1843; its skin-lightening effect was first reported in 1936.[3] In 1975 Kligman tested the combination with tretinoin and dexamethasone for melasma and related conditions.[3] The US FDA classified hydroquinone as generally recognised as safe and effective in 1982, revoked that in 2006 and banned over-the-counter use in 2020.[3]

Registered trials compare the triple cream with alternatives or add-ons: mometasone-based versions, the Westerhoff formula, topical metformin, oral tranexamic acid, microneedling and platelet-rich plasma.[12][13][14][15] Their results are not yet summarised in published sources reviewed here.

The 2005 12-month study of 228 patients and the 2025 randomised trial against Tri-Luma in Chinese patients are the principal studies of the fluocinolone version.[1][9] A 2022 randomised trial examined oral tranexamic acid with the cream, and a 2007 analysis examined cost-effectiveness against hydroquinone alone.[8][10] A trial listing for solar lentigines (2008, n=22) is also registered.[6]
